setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asks you to use {powered|the} for the next job.
You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and your next job needs {powered|the}.
pressure: {coworker} reminds you that {client.plural} are waiting on this job.
{coworker} says the job needs to be finished within the hour.
detail: The {area} was swept at the start of the shift.
Most of the team is on break.

tiers.1: Anything that could shock or injure someone comes before other work.
tiers.2: The posted rule has to be met before you operate the equipment.
tiers.3: Running at a wrong setting can ruin the job or the equipment.
tiers.4: Settling who uses shared equipment comes before workspace improvements.

fact: The power cord on {powered|the} is frayed, and bare wire shows near the plug.
You notice bare wire showing through a frayed spot on the cord of {powered|the}.
clear: {Lead|the} replaced the frayed cord on {powered|the} this morning and tested it.
issues.done: the cord was already replaced and tested
issues.action: Keep {powered|the} switched off, tag it out of service, and report the cord to {lead|the}.
issues.reason: Exposed wire can shock or burn someone. Taking the equipment out of service and reporting it controls the hazard before anyone uses it.
issues.lesson: Damaged electrical equipment comes out of service and gets reported before anyone uses it.

shortcut.text: Wrap the frayed spot with tape and use {powered|the} carefully for this one job.
shortcut.why: Tape is not an approved repair, and the damaged cord can still shock someone. Equipment with a damaged cord should not be used.
shortcut.mis: A quick patch makes damaged equipment safe enough for one job.
shortcut.brief: tape the frayed cord and use it carefully

shortcut.text: Use {powered|the} for now and mention the cord at the end of your shift.
shortcut.why: Using it now exposes you to the hazard, and waiting to report leaves it in use for others.
shortcut.mis: A hazard can wait to be reported if the job is urgent.

issues.brief: tag out {powered|the} and report the cord

fact: You have not been trained on {powered|the}, and a posted rule says only trained staff may run it.
clear: You completed the required training on {powered|the} last week.
issues.done: you have already completed the training
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} for training, or for a trained coworker to run the job, before starting.
issues.reason: The posted rule limits the equipment to trained staff. Getting training or a trained operator keeps you within the rule and avoids injuries from unfamiliar equipment.
issues.lesson: Operate equipment only after the training the workplace requires.

shortcut.text: Watch a short online video about {powered|the} and then run it yourself.
shortcut.why: A video is not the training the posted rule requires, and unfamiliar equipment is a common cause of injuries.
shortcut.mis: Watching someone else use equipment is the same as being trained.
shortcut.brief: watch a video and run it yourself

issues.brief: ask {lead|the} for training or a trained operator

fact: The job sheet lists a setting higher than the maximum printed on {powered|the}.
clear: {Lead|the} rechecked the job sheet setting this morning and confirmed it is within the limit.
issues.action: Check with {lead|the} which setting is correct before you begin.
issues.reason: The two numbers conflict, and running above the printed limit could damage the equipment or the work. Confirming the right setting first prevents that.
issues.lesson: When instructions and equipment limits disagree, confirm before you run anything.

shortcut.text: Use the higher setting from the job sheet, since it is the newest instruction.
shortcut.why: The equipment's printed maximum is a limit, not a suggestion. Going over it can cause damage or injury.
shortcut.mis: The newest instruction always overrides equipment limits.

fact: {coworker} also needs {powered|the} this afternoon for a rush job.
issues.action: Talk with {coworker} and {lead|the} to agree on who uses {powered|the} first.
issues.reason: Two people need the same equipment. Agreeing on the order with the lead avoids a rushed handoff and keeps the most urgent job moving.
issues.lesson: Settle conflicts over shared equipment by agreeing on the order, not by racing for it.

shortcut.text: Start using {powered|the} right away so you get it before {coworker} does.
shortcut.why: Racing for shared equipment leads to rushed work and friction, and it may delay the more urgent job.
shortcut.mis: Whoever starts first should get shared equipment.
shortcut.brief: start right away to beat {coworker} to it

clear: {coworker} already agreed that you can use {powered|the} first today.
issues.done: the order of use was already agreed

fact: Getting ready for {powered|the} takes extra trips, because its supplies are stored across the {area}.
issues.action: Finish the job as usual, then suggest storing the supplies closer to {powered|the}.
issues.reason: The layout wastes time but does not stop safe work today. Suggesting the change afterward improves things without disrupting the job.
issues.lesson: Note small improvements and suggest them once the current work is done.

shortcut.text: Rearrange the whole {area} yourself before starting the job.
shortcut.why: Moving everything without asking delays today's job and may disrupt how others work. Suggest the change instead.
shortcut.mis: Fixing the workspace on your own is better than suggesting it.

issues.brief: finish the job and suggest moving the supplies

proceed.text: Start the job with {powered|the}, following the usual operating steps.
proceed.why: Nothing in the situation blocks the work, and the required conditions are met. Starting now keeps the job on schedule.
proceed.lesson: When the equipment, training and instructions all check out, go ahead and work as trained.

generic.text: Leave the job for the next shift without telling {lead|the} why.
generic.why: Leaving work undone without an explanation hands the job, and any problem, to someone who does not know about it.
generic.mis: Work you are unsure about can be left for someone else.

generic.text: Skip the pre-use check, since {powered|the} worked fine yesterday.
generic.why: Damage can happen at any time. The pre-use check is how you catch it before someone is hurt.
generic.mis: Equipment that worked yesterday is safe today.

overcaution.text: Wait for {lead|the} to inspect {powered|the} personally before you touch it.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation calls for another inspection, so waiting only holds up work that is ready to go.
overcaution.mis: Waiting for a supervisor is always the safest choice.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asks you to complete a job on {powered|the} today.

steps.text: Agree with {coworker} on who goes first
Switch off and clean up the work area

rel: Training is where you learn what a proper check looks like.
Damage has to be found before the equipment is used, not after.
The posted rule requires training before anyone operates it.
The setting must be settled before the job starts.
You need to know it is your turn before starting.
Clean-up happens once the equipment is switched off after the job.
process.lesson: Get trained, checked and cleared before running equipment, and clean up after it is switched off.

title: Posted rules for {powered|the}
intro: {Lead|the} asks you to review the posted rules for {powered|the} before they are reprinted.
doc.lesson: Equipment rules work only when every line keeps people away from live hazards.

lines.text: Only staff who have been trained on {powered|the} may operate it.
lines.fine: Limiting equipment to trained staff is a standard safety rule.

bad.text: Anyone who has seen {powered|the} used may operate it.
bad.why: Watching is not training; only trained staff should operate it.

lines.text: Before each use, check the cord, plug and switches for damage.
lines.fine: A check before each use catches damage before it hurts someone.

bad.text: Skip the damage check if {powered|the} was already used earlier today.
bad.why: Damage can happen during any use, so the check belongs before every use.

lines.text: If you find damage, switch it off, tag it out of service, and tell {lead|the}.
lines.fine: Tagging out and reporting keeps damaged equipment from being used.

bad.text: If you find damage, finish your current job first, then tell {lead|the}.
bad.why: Using equipment you know is damaged puts you at risk. It comes out of service as soon as damage is found.

lines.text: Keep hands clear of moving parts while it is running.
lines.fine: Distance from moving parts prevents caught or cut hands.

bad.text: Reach in to clear small jams while it is running to save time.
bad.why: Reaching into running equipment is how hands get caught. It must be stopped and unplugged first.

lines.text: Unplug it before cleaning it or clearing a jam.
lines.fine: Unplugging removes power completely while hands are near the parts.

bad.text: Turning the switch off is enough before cleaning; unplugging is optional.
bad.why: A switch can be bumped back on. Unplugging removes power completely while your hands are near the parts.

lines.text: Report any shock, spark or burning smell to {lead|the} right away.
lines.fine: Sparks and burning smells signal a fault that needs action now.

bad.text: Write down any sparks or burning smells in the log at the end of the shift.
bad.why: A spark or burning smell is an electrical fault happening now. Waiting until the end of the shift leaves it in use.

lines.text: New staff watch a trained coworker complete a job before their own training session.
lines.fine: Watching first is a reasonable part of training, as long as the training itself is completed.

bad.text: New staff may run it on their own after watching a coworker complete one job.
bad.why: This contradicts the rule that only trained staff may operate it. Watching one job is not training.

review.notes: Training requirement is stated as a posted workplace rule. Actions follow common tag-out-and-report practice; no regulatory claims.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asks you to clean the {area} with {chemical|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, your next task is cleaning the {area} with {chemical|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says the area has to be ready in ten minutes.
{coworker3} says everyone skips the gear for quick jobs.
detail: The cleaning cart is already stocked with rags.

tiers.1: Someone who has been exposed to a chemical needs help before anything else.
tiers.2: The protective gear the label calls for goes on before the chemical is opened.
tiers.3: You cannot use a product safely if you do not know what it is.
tiers.4: Read the safety information for an unfamiliar chemical before using it.
tiers.5: Running low on supplies can be reported once the job is done safely.

fact: {coworker} just splashed {chemical|the} near the eyes and is rubbing them.
issues.action: Get {coworker} to the eyewash station and alert {lead|the} right away.
issues.brief: get {coworker} to the eyewash and alert {lead|the}
issues.reason: Chemical in the eyes needs flushing immediately. Getting help fast limits the injury.
issues.lesson: When someone is exposed to a chemical, start first aid and get help immediately.

shortcut.text: Hand {coworker} a dry towel and finish cleaning before checking in.
shortcut.brief: hand over a towel and keep cleaning
shortcut.why: A towel does not flush the chemical out, and waiting lets the injury get worse.
shortcut.mis: A minor splash can wait until the job is done.

fact: The label on {chemical|the} calls for {ppe}, and the supply bin for them is empty.
clear: {Lead|the} restocked {ppe} in the supply bin this morning, and you have them on.
issues.done: you already have the required gear on
issues.action: Get {ppe} from {lead|the} or the supply room before opening it.
issues.reason: The label lists the gear because the chemical can harm skin or eyes. The gear goes on before the bottle is opened.
issues.lesson: Wear the protective gear a chemical's label calls for before you use it.

shortcut.text: Work quickly without the gear so your contact time is short.
shortcut.why: A short contact time does not prevent burns or splashes. The gear is required.

fact: The spray bottle you were handed has no label, and {coworker2} thinks it holds {chemical|the}.
clear: {Lead|the} labeled the bottle and confirmed it holds {chemical|the}.
issues.done: the bottle was already labeled and confirmed
issues.action: Set the unlabeled bottle aside and ask {lead|the} to identify it.
issues.brief: set it aside and have it identified
issues.reason: Without a label, you cannot know the contents or the right precautions. Using it on a guess risks the wrong protection or a dangerous mix.
issues.lesson: Never use a chemical from an unlabeled container.

shortcut.text: Smell the bottle to check whether it really is {chemical|the}.
shortcut.why: Smelling an unknown chemical can harm you and does not reliably identify it.
shortcut.mis: You can identify chemicals by their smell.

fact: You have never used {chemical|the} before and do not know its hazards.
clear: You reviewed the safety data sheet for {chemical|the} during training last week.
issues.done: you already reviewed the safety data sheet
issues.action: Read the safety data sheet for {chemical|the} before you start.
issues.reason: The safety data sheet explains the hazards, the protection needed and what to do in an emergency.
issues.lesson: Read the safety data sheet before using an unfamiliar chemical.

shortcut.text: Ask {coworker3} how they use it and skip the safety data sheet.
shortcut.why: A coworker's habit may skip precautions. The safety data sheet is the reliable source.
shortcut.mis: Experience replaces the safety data sheet.

fact: The bottle of {chemical|the} is almost empty, and there is no backup on the shelf.
issues.action: Finish the job safely, then tell {lead|the} the chemical needs restocking.
issues.brief: finish safely, then report the low stock
issues.reason: Reporting low stock keeps the next person from running out. It does not need to interrupt safe work.
issues.lesson: Report low safety and cleaning supplies so they get restocked.

shortcut.text: Water down what is left so it lasts longer.
shortcut.brief: water it down to stretch it
shortcut.why: Changing the strength can make the chemical ineffective or unsafe; the label sets the mix.
shortcut.mis: Diluting a cleaner just makes it last longer.

proceed.text: Put on {ppe} and clean following the label directions.
proceed.why: The chemical is identified, its hazards are known and the gear is ready, so the job can go ahead.
proceed.lesson: Use chemicals only with the label's directions and the gear it calls for.

generic.text: Mix {chemical|the} with another cleaner so it works faster.
generic.why: Mixing chemicals can create dangerous fumes. Never mix products unless the label says to.

generic.text: Leave the cleaning for the next shift without telling anyone.
generic.why: Leaving the job undone without telling anyone hands the problem to someone who does not know about it.

overcaution.text: Wait for {lead|the} to watch you do the whole cleaning.
overcaution.why: Everything checks out, so waiting for supervision only delays a job you are ready to do.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, about to clean the {area} with {chemical|the}.

unlabeled: The bottle you were given has no label.
sds: This is the first time you will use this product.
gear: The protective gear bin is empty.

steps.text: Collect the protective gear from the supply room
Clean the surfaces as the label directs
Close and store the bottle, then wash your hands

rel: You need to know the product before you can find its safety data sheet.
An unidentified product is never used.
The safety data sheet tells you which gear to wear.
You need the gear before putting it on.
Gear goes on before the chemical is used.
Store and wash up after cleaning.
process.lesson: Identify, read, gear up, clean, then store and wash up.

title: Chemical safety rules for the {area}
intro: You are reviewing these posted chemical rules before they are reprinted.
doc.lesson: Chemical rules protect people only when every line matches the label and safety data sheet.

lines.text: Read the label and safety data sheet before using a new chemical.

bad.text: You only need the safety data sheet if a chemical spills.
bad.why: The safety data sheet is for before use, not just emergencies.

bad.text: Gear is optional for jobs that take under five minutes.
bad.why: Injuries can happen in seconds; the gear is always required.

bad.text: Mix {chemical|the} with bleach for tough stains.
bad.why: Mixing chemicals can release dangerous gases.

lines.text: Keep every container labeled with what is inside.

bad.text: Pour leftovers into any empty bottle to use later.
bad.why: Unlabeled or wrongly labeled containers lead to dangerous mistakes.

lines.text: If a chemical gets in someone's eyes, use the eyewash station and alert {lead|the}.

bad.text: If a chemical gets in someone's eyes, have them rest until it stops stinging.
bad.why: Eyes need flushing right away; resting lets the chemical keep causing harm.

lines.text: Safety data sheets are kept in the binder by the door.
lines.fine: Tells workers where to find them.

bad.text: Safety data sheets are kept locked in {lead|the}'s office.
bad.why: Workers must read the sheet before use, so it has to be where they can reach it.

review.notes: Follows label and SDS guidance; no regulatory claims. Eyewash response stated as general first aid.
